The wrong_population hypothesis is plausible — early-stage patients with lower tumor burden and less established endocrine resistance may not benefit from mTOR inhibition the way metastatic patients do. 5. CONFOUNDERS: The trial was adequately powered (N=1939), had a long follow-up (up to 10 years), and used an appropriate comparator. The placebo arm performed well (74.4% IDFS), which is consistent with the early-stage adjuvant setting where hormone therapy alone is highly effective. The high baseline efficacy of hormone therapy in early-stage disease may have left little room for improvement (ceiling effect). The safety burden of everolimus was substantial, with markedly higher rates of mucositis, metabolic disturbances, pneumonitis, and serious cardiac events, but the structured AE data does not show evidence that dose-limiting toxicity prevented adequate dosing — the trial ran its full course. The primary failure mode is biology_moved_endpoint_flat / wrong_population: the mTOR pathway may have been engaged (indirect evidence from metabolic AEs), but mTOR inhibition did not translate to improved IDFS in this early-stage adjuvant population, likely because the mechanism of endocrine resistance reversal is not relevant in treatment-naive early-stage disease.
